subject: biology
title: Ecosystems, communities and interdependence
key_idea: An **ecosystem** is a community of living organisms interacting with the non-living parts of their environment. Organisms **compete** for resources and depend on each other for food, shelter and pollination. In a **stable community** population sizes stay fairly constant.

blocks.text: Ecology studies how living things fit into their surroundings. This section covers the levels from a single organism up to a whole ecosystem.

items.meaning: All the organisms of one species living in an area.
All the populations of different species living in the same area.
The place where an organism lives.
The interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment.

items: Organisms need a supply of materials from their surroundings and from the other living organisms there.
These materials let them survive and reproduce.
A pond, a woodland and a lawn are all ecosystems.

diagram.alt: Put the levels of organisation in order, from a single organism up to a whole ecosystem.
diagram.prompt: Put these levels of organisation in order, from smallest to largest.

items: A population is one species. A community is all the species in an area.
An ecosystem is the community plus its non-living surroundings.

blocks.text: Organisms in a community share limited resources. This section covers what they compete for and how they depend on each other.

items.meaning: When organisms need the same limited resource, so there is not enough for all of them.
Each species depends on other species for things such as food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal.

rows: Light, space, water and mineral ions from the soil

items: If one species is removed, it can affect the whole community.
For example, if a predator is removed its prey may increase, and then eat too much of their own food.
Animals that are predators can control the size of a prey population.
Some species provide shelter or spread pollen and seeds for others.

blocks.text: In a **stable community** all the species and environmental factors are in balance. Population sizes stay fairly constant.
A garden is not stable, because organisms are always being added or removed.

items: Plants compete for light, space, water and mineral ions. Animals compete for food, mates and territory.
Interdependence means removing one species can affect the whole community.
A stable community has fairly constant population sizes.

blocks.text: Some species depend on each other in a close, long-term relationship. This section covers two kinds: parasitism and mutualism.

items.meaning: An organism that lives on or in another organism (the host) and feeds on it, harming it.
The organism a parasite lives on or in.
A relationship where both organisms benefit.

diagram.alt: A comparison of parasitism and mutualism by who benefits and who is harmed.

values: Mites feeding on the blood of a slug. Mistletoe growing on a tree.
A fly eats algae. Bacteria in its gut digest the algae, so the fly gets nutrients. The bacteria get an acidic gut to live in.

items: A parasite gains food or water from the host, and the host is damaged.
In mutualism each partner gets something it needs, such as food or a place to live.
Both relationships are examples of interdependence.
A parasite lives on or in a host and harms it.

checks.q: Give two factors that plants compete for in a habitat.
checks.a: Any two from: (sun)light, water, ions / minerals / salts, space.

checks.q: Explain what is meant by the term parasite.
checks.a: An organism that lives on or in a host organism and feeds on it. It benefits at the expense of (harms) its host.

checks.q: Explain why a garden is not a stable community.
checks.a: Organisms / species are always being added or removed, so population sizes are not fairly constant.

worked_example.question:
Genetic engineering can also be used in agriculture. Weeds are a problem for farmers because the weeds compete with crop plants.

Give three factors that the weeds and crop plants compete for.
worked_example.tip: Any three score one mark each. A named example, such as a named mineral ion, is allowed.

worked_example.question:
Tiny white animals called mites live on the skin of a slug. The mites feed on blood.

Explain why these mites are classed as parasites.
answer_points: Parasites live in or on their host. The mites live on the slug, which is the host.
Parasites feed off their host. The mites feed on the slug by sucking its blood.
worked_example.tip: One mark for living on or in the host and one for feeding on it.

worked_example.question:
Many people grow buddleia bushes in their gardens. Buddleia flowers attract butterflies that feed on nectar. Birds and bats feed on butterflies. Foxes and badgers can live under the cover of the bushes. Buddleia bushes spread and grow very quickly. In some areas this has caused the numbers of other plants to decrease. In these areas, scientists have seen large numbers of butterflies. However, they only see the more common types of butterflies and not rare ones.

Some scientists say buddleia are 'pests' but others say they are 'friends'. Use information from the passage to explain these different opinions about buddleia. In your answer use ideas about interdependence, competition and biodiversity.
answer_points: Friend: butterflies depend on buddleia for food, and birds and bats depend on butterflies.
Friend: foxes and badgers depend on buddleia for cover, and without it they would be more vulnerable to weather and predators.
Buddleia are the producers in the food chains.
Pest: buddleia outcompetes other plants, which lack light, water, minerals or space, so their numbers decrease.
Pest: buddleia has reduced biodiversity, because there is less variety of types of butterflies and plants.
worked_example.tip: Marked by level. The top level needs both positive and negative actions of buddleia, each explained, in a clear logical order.
